title: Common partner counts gave no clear connection prediction gain in selected Allen mouse and human slices
abstract: We tested whether common input and output partners improve prediction of a detected chemical connection after other measured wiring features are known. We used Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1 and excluded whole inferred donors from fitting. The samples had 18,906 mouse VisP directions from 732 inferred donors and 1,456 human TCx directions from 42 inferred donors. Base models used cell labels, distance, probe counts, the reverse call, local marginal connection counts, and recording density. Adding common partner counts gave log-loss gains of -0.000100 and -0.001553 nats per direction. Conditional 97.5% donor intervals were [-0.000371, 0.000161] and [-0.003547, 0.000404]. Neither primary test gave a clear gain. With local marginal counts fixed, either overlap count could vary in only 8.65% of mouse directions and 12.64% of human directions. This is a conditional completion benchmark, not a test of unmeasured whole circuits or neural activity. Sparse overlap, slice detection, inferred donor labels, model choice, and intervals that omit refit uncertainty limit inference. We supply selected calls, predictions, overlap bounds, source hashes, code, figures, and an independent audit.

display.caption: Common input and output counts gave no clear primary log-loss gain. Points show mean gain across three five-fold donor allocations. Bars show conditional 97.5% donor bootstrap intervals. They omit model refit uncertainty. Positive gain means better prediction.

Most eligible pairs have overlap fixed by sparse local marginal counts. Orange bars count directions for which common input can vary within elementary intersection bounds; they are not independent sample sizes. Blue bars include zero-partner directions from the selected cohort.
